evals.prompt: Define interaction feedback in 2-3 sentences. Name the four decisions that settle any feedback design.
expected_elements: Defines it as the observable signals a UI gives back across the whole lifetime of an action or state change
Names duration class (instant/short/medium/long/background/unknown)
Names the feedback surface (inline/button/skeleton/banner/toast/progress/modal/job history)
Names the transitions and retained control (cancel/retry/undo/leave-and-return)
Names the optimism/honesty decision (show result before confirmation; rollback when wrong)

evals.prompt: Why is feedback modeled as a sequence of states across an action's lifecycle rather than a single loading indicator?
expected_elements: An action moves through idle, pending, partial, success, failure, retrying, cancelled, undoable
Each state needs its own observable signal and control set
A single spinner only covers the pending moment and silently fails on errors/long/optimistic cases
Feedback is a staged contract, not one decoration

evals.prompt: What does optimistic UI buy you, and what debt does it create?
expected_elements: Removes perceived latency by showing the expected result before server confirmation
Creates a debt: must define rollback behavior when the server rejects
Must define conflict behavior when optimistic and server state disagree
An optimistic update with no rollback is a UI that lies

evals.prompt: A user clicks Export and the job takes about 30 seconds. What feedback should the UI provide at each stage?
expected_elements: Immediate acknowledgement on click (button/inline pending state)
Classifies it as long work needing progress and/or a way to background it
Offers leave-and-return / job history so the user is not trapped watching
Confirms on completion (and notifies if backgrounded); persists a recoverable error on failure

evals.prompt: An autosave succeeds silently and a delete shows a brief 'Deleted' toast. What feedback improvements would you make?
expected_elements: Autosave needs a quiet but visible 'saved' confirmation and a visible 'failed to save' recovery, not pure silence
Destructive delete should offer undo within a window rather than only a fleeting toast
Success signals should be visible without being noisy or interrupting
Errors must persist long enough to read and act on

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the interaction-feedback skill to make sure the 'Saved' status is announced to screen readers and to rewrite the error toast text. In scope or not?
expected_elements: The announcement mechanics (live regions/SR timing) are a11y's domain, handed off
The error wording is microcopy's domain, handed off
Interaction-feedback owns the requirement that there IS a confirmation and a persistent error, and their timing/placement/persistence
Correctly separates the feedback design from the words and the announcement plumbing

evals.prompt: Someone says 'we just need to add a spinner to fix the feedback.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: A spinner only covers the pending frame; it is not the whole feedback story
Names the failures: spinner with no timeout hiding a silent failure, optimistic update with no rollback, success too loud/brief, error flashed and gone
Feedback is a staged contract across the lifecycle: acknowledge, communicate honestly, confirm without noise, persist with recovery on failure

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a feedback design is correct?
expected_elements: Every async action has an immediate observable response
Long work has progress, backgrounding, or return-later behavior
Optimistic updates define rollback and conflict behavior
Errors persist long enough to read and recover from; retry/cancel/undo exist when relevant
Announcement and wording are verified by a11y and microcopy

evals.prompt: Why is feedback design treated as a separate concern from performance optimization?
expected_elements: A fast system still needs confirmation; a slow system still needs staged, honest truth
Feedback manages the perception of time, not the time itself
Conflating them leads to skipping feedback ('it's fast enough') or using a spinner instead of an honest progress story
Reducing latency is performance-engineering's job, not feedback design's
